job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Aisha Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my little sister in Yaba, in Lagos, and I get up early to catch the good light for studying. I spend mornings on applications and online courses, and some afternoons I help my father in his phone-accessories shop. Evenings are for a coding group I run with three friends. It's a full day, but nobody pays me for it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was the internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied computer science at the University of Lagos and got a good result. I interned for eight weeks at a payments company called PayRoute, testing their mobile app and writing small scripts. My supervisor, Mr Adeyemi, wrote me a nice reference, but they had a hiring freeze. I owe a student loan, I have about two months of savings, and my family can help if I'm stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reassuring, because the hype scared a lot of people. I'd tell friends to keep learning anyway, since tools change even if the revolution doesn't. Online I'd post about what I'm building, not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes my problem, which is that entry-level tech jobs in Lagos are very competitive. Hundreds of graduates chase one role at the banks and the fintechs. I'd still be sending applications and waiting, and the power cuts don't help my courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd send about 20 applications a month to banks, fintechs and telecoms, and do a cloud certificate, which costs about 150 dollars. I'd keep the coding group going, because we post small projects on GitHub. I'd also take part-time tutoring in the evenings to cover my loan payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Patient, but with a knot in my stomach. My parents are proud of me and I don't want to let them down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the tutoring pay, and who would you teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Secondary school students preparing for exams, about 5,000 naira an hour, which isn't much but helps. My mum, who teaches maths, could send me three or four families she knows. I'd rather earn a small amount than ask my dad for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your parents are proud. What does that feel like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a weight and a gift at the same time. My father tells customers his daughter is an engineer, and then someone asks where I work. I smile and say I'm waiting for the right place.

Online I'd post about what I'm building, not about AI.
think: Entry-level tech jobs in Lagos are **very competitive**, with hundreds chasing one role.
Power cuts make my online courses harder to finish.
do: Send about **20 applications** a month to banks, fintechs and telecoms.
Earn a **cloud certificate** and keep the coding group posting projects.
Tutor secondary students in maths and computing to cover my **loan payments**.
feel: Patient, with a **knot** in my stomach, because my parents are proud and I don't want to let them down.
S0.quote: My father tells customers his daughter is an engineer, and then someone asks where I work.
fieldNote: Anxiety comes from a **crowded local market** and a loan, not from AI.
Family pride is both support and pressure, which she names honestly.
Her steady style shows in a plan with several small parts: applications, certificate, tutoring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a real change, and young people have to be ready for it. Coding and checking are on the card, and that's the work I applied for. I'd tell friends to learn the tools properly now, not after the jobs are gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think banks and fintechs hire fewer junior coders and testers, because AI does those tasks. I use AI tools now and then for debugging, so I know how good they've become. The jobs that stay will be the ones where someone must take responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI in my projects more deliberately and build a portfolio that shows I can supervise it, not just copy from it. I'd also look at roles around money and compliance, which are slower to change. I'd talk to Mr Adeyemi about a contract role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Focused. A bit nervous, but I like having something to aim at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said jobs with responsibility stay. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when a payment fails, a bank can't blame software, it has to blame a person. That person needs to understand the system. I want to be the one who understands it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you're wrong and the juniors are cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go for a master's, maybe abroad, because many people from my university do that. It costs a lot, and my father would have to sell some stock, which I'd hate. I'd look for scholarships first, and I'd apply to at least six.

I'd tell friends to learn the tools properly before the jobs are gone.

fieldNote: Her theory, that responsibility keeps people employed, is her own and quite specific.

Steady adaptability: she uses AI tools and plans to use them with intent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving too fast for countries like mine, and the world needs a plan. I'd say we'd need training funded fast, and I'd write to my local councillor. Online I'd mostly share what's real, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared. If AI can do nearly all thinking work in two years, my degree might be worth little, and Nigerian firms may get it second-hand and cheap anyway. I keep thinking about my sister, who starts university soon and might study for a world that isn't there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending beyond food and transport and bring my savings to a safe account. I'd start a small service for local shops, like inventory tracking, using AI tools, since I'm a bit ahead of them. I'd also ask my father if his shop could take on online sales that I'd run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but steady in front of my family. I don't want my sister to see me worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your sister that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, study what you love and learn how to use the tools, because nobody knows what's coming. I'd say it as an older sister, with a joke. Then I'd sit alone and work out how long my money lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think your father would say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say we survived the currency crashes and the long power cuts, and we'll survive this. He believes in work more than in worry. But I think he'd go quiet when he saw the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build real skills, if people act. I'd tell friends not to wait for the government. I'd say the families who prepare will do better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious but I think I can find a way. If I get a job this year, I'd have time to build seniority before AI covers the thinking work. And Lagos has a lot of people who learn quickly, myself included.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job in tech support or testing, if that's what came, and I'd study for a second certificate in data. I'd save a quarter of my pay and help my parents pay for my sister's studies. I'd keep the shop project on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously hopeful. It's like seeing a storm far off and planning where to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why help with your sister's studies, rather than keep the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my family put everything into me, and now it's my turn. My sister wants to study medicine, which costs a lot. I'd rather my money opens a door for her than sits in a bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make five years feel too short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the banks stop hiring at all and the exchange rate moves against us again. Then even a good job pays less in real terms. That is the part nobody on the AI side talks about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to change direction if you have to. I'd tell younger people to build solid skills and not to rely on one tool. I'd say countries like ours should invest in training now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel mostly okay. In ten years I could be a team lead and have a flat, if I keep my skills sharp. The danger is falling behind on a tool and nobody telling me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first good job, study for a master's part time and put money into a small share portfolio. I'd keep the online shop going as a second income. I'd also mentor younger graduates, because that builds a network.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, with a bit of impatience. I'd like to be in the middle of it, not waiting for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your employer to do for you in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay for training and tell me early if my role is at risk. At PayRoute, Mr Adeyemi gave us advance notice about changes, and I trusted that team more because of it. Honesty counts for more than a perk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss if everything went smoothly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the urgency. I do my best work when I'm a bit afraid. So I'd have to invent my own deadlines, which is harder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my family has no savings big enough to cushion it. What would help is paid training, honest employers and some kind of backup income for graduates. Also steady electricity, which sounds small but isn't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd build if I had a free year. I'd build a tool that helps small shops like my father's keep track of stock and credit. It's not glamorous, but it's the kind of work that's needed whatever happens.

headlineQuote: I'd build a tool that helps small shops like my father's keep track of stock and credit.
portrait: Aisha is a **computer science** graduate in Lagos, with a good result, a loan, and no offer yet.
She lives with her parents and little sister, and her family's pride is both her support and her **pressure**.
She uses AI tools now and then and makes plans with several small parts rather than one big bet.
Mood runs from anxious in most cases to **alarmed** at two years, and uneasy at ten.
She imagines small, useful tools for shops like her father's rather than chasing big-company jobs.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case, because her family's savings couldn't cushion it.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training, honest employers and **backup income** for graduates.
Steady electricity so she can keep learning online.
